extracted.intended_audience: political scientists, administrative law scholars, and researchers studying public participation, interest-group mobilization, and federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Theory-driven empirical guidance for identifying, classifying, and evaluating mass public comment / pressure campaigns that target agency rulemaking, with attention to who mobilizes, what information is produced, and how campaigns influence bureaucratic policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizer type (who mobilizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two competing expectations: (1) groups with more resources will dominate public pressure campaigns (mirror typical interest-group lobbying); (2) groups with fewer material resources but broader popular support will more often use public pressure campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observable implications of each theory to classify campaign sponsors. If resource-rich groups dominate, campaigns likely reinforce existing power; if groups with popular support dominate, campaigns may expand representation. Empirically assess organizer characteristics (resources, membership, past lobbying behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest type: public interest groups vs private/industry sponsors
rubrics_metrics.description: Public interest advocacy groups are predicted to launch pressure campaigns more often than private/industry interests; private interests sponsor campaigns only under limited conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect advocacy organizations to produce larger, more frequent campaigns. Industry-sponsored campaigns tend to be smaller and less likely to identify the sponsor; industry campaigns are also more often contesting advocacy campaigns rather than acting alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources and organizing capacity (concentration of mobilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resources required to run campaigns concentrate mobilizing capacity in a few large organizations; empirically, a small number of advocacy organizations generate the bulk of comments (e.g., 100 organizations mobilized over 80% of comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure concentration of mobilizers (Gini, top-N share). High concentration implies that participatory processes may still be driven by a small set of powerful organizers despite large comment counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political information produced by campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comments produce political information (information about the distribution and intensity of policy preferences and demands) distinct from technical/legal expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns on how they reveal distribution/intensity of opinions (numbers, geographic/ demographic distribution) rather than novel technical claims. Recognize this as information valuable to policymakers for gauging political risk and support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of support: genuine mobilization vs astroturf
rubrics_metrics.description: Astroturf campaigns intentionally project false or inflated grassroots support; genuine mobilization demonstrates real supporters. Astroturf undermines the credibility of the political information provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for anonymity, lack of linkage to known lobbying organizations, and suspicious patterns of submission as signals of astroturf. Theorized to be rare because faking support risks reputational harm for groups that also engage in sophisticated lobbying; policymakers rationally discount anonymous or unknown sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale / number of comments (mass participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheer number of comments can dramatically increase public attention and indicate an issue's salience; online mobilization has enabled thousands to millions of comments on some rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify comment volume and compare to baseline rulemaking attention. Use volume as a measure of salience and potential political pressure, but interpret alongside content quality and sponsor credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment content quality: deliberation, technical sophistication, or mere aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments vary from deliberative, informed, technical submissions to aggregated, non-deliberative expressions of preference (mass form letters). Deliberative/technical comments are more likely to contain novel policy-relevant information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comments for technical/legal content versus simple expressions of support/opposition. Expect agencies to cite and act on technical/legal comments more often than mass, non-technical submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form letters / template comments vs individualized comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Form letters differ qualitatively from individualized comments; empirical work finds form letters are cited less often and less associated with policy change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify form-letter patterns (near-duplicate text, templated fields). Analyze whether campaigns rely on form letters or encourage tailored input; treat form-letter-heavy campaigns as weaker sources of novel information to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition structure and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass mobilization should be conceptualized as a tactic within coalition lobbying; the unit of analysis can be the lobbying coalition rather than single organizations, and comments should be attributed to coalitions that mobilized them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding campaigns, identify coalitions and attribute mobilized comments to the coalition(s) that produced the campaign. Consider coalition formation (partners, lead organizations) as a feature influencing reach and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsorship identification and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a campaign identifies its sponsoring organization(s) affects credibility; industry campaigns are less likely to identify sponsors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether comments or campaign materials clearly identify sponsoring organizations. Anonymous or obscured sponsorship reduces the persuasive value of mass comments for policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue expertise / agency reliance on technical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies that rely more heavily on specialized expertise tend to receive fewer public comments; rules perceived as less open to influence attract more mobilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for the technical/expert nature of the rule when comparing comment volumes across rulemakings. Expect issue areas with high technical barriers to have lower mass-public mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of conflict expansion (going public / outside strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure campaigns are a form of 'going public'—expanding the scope of conflict beyond the usual cadre of political actors to mobilize broader publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns on whether they meaningfully expand conflict scope (new audiences, media attention, protests) versus targeting usual insiders. Use measures of outreach tactics (press releases, phonebanking, public events) and resulting audience composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and 'second‑order representation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations often claim to represent broad constituencies; mobilized comments serve as evidence of representation but can be cheap talk if unsubstantiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well mobilized commenters map to claimed constituencies (membership lists, verifiable supporter data). Treat demonstrated grassroots action as stronger evidence of representational claims than raw membership numbers or unverifiable assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan alignment and political skew
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobilizing organizations are often partisan in alignment; large national advocacy groups in the dataset skew strongly Democratic, affecting the partisan balance of public participation under different administrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure partisan alignment of mobilizers and resulting comment support. Account for administration party when analyzing whether public pressure supports or opposes agency proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience and attention-raising effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure campaigns frequently increase public attention to agency policies by several orders of magnitude; many people only learn about bureaucratic policymaking via campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use media mentions, protest size, and comment spikes to operationalize salience increases. Recognize that heightened salience can change political incentives facing agency officials and elected overseers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on rulemaking outcomes and process (influence and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comments may affect agencies (e.g., citation rates, policy change) and procedural aspects (e.g., time to final rule); prior studies find mixed evidence—agencies often discard non-technical comments and form letters are less associated with change, though some research links mass comments to longer processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically test associations between campaign features (volume, content, sponsor credibility) and outcomes: citations in rulemaking records, revisions in final rules, and delay/extension of rulemaking timelines. Beware confounding by issue salience and pre-existing political controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of claims vs aggregation of preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions and mass comments can either bring new substantive claims (novel issues, facts) or simply aggregate preferences numerically; petitions can serve as a vehicle for 'new claims' beyond elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code comments for presence of novel substantive claims or technical information versus mere expressions of support/opposition. Prioritize identification of new factual or technical information as higher-value for policymaking.
